heading: Practise for Georgia's State Language Exam.
lead: Timed practice papers for the listening, reading and writing parts of the State Language Exam (სახელმწიფო ენის გამოცდა), for test A (levels A1 and A2) and test B (levels B1 and B2). Behind them is a complete Georgian course from the script to C1, so you can work on whatever the papers show you are missing.

sections.heading: What the exam asks
intro: The exam certifies how well a person knows Georgian. The National Assessment and Examinations Center (NAEC, შეფასებისა და გამოცდების ეროვნული ცენტრი) runs it in Tbilisi, and the State Language Department issues the certificate to those who pass. It is voluntary and open to anyone who registers; the fee, as the decree set it in 2025, is 50 lari.

There are two tests: test A decides A1 or A2 and test B decides B1 or B2, depending on your points. Each has four parts of 25 points. Listening, reading and writing share 2 hours 30 minutes, of which 40 minutes are for listening; speaking takes 9 minutes after a short break.
rows: 25 questions on recordings heard twice. In test A, short announcements with true-or-false statements and short dialogues with three answers; in test B, opinions matched to speakers and other tasks with up to four options.
All 25 questions in the real test's numbers of options, in 40 minutes.
25 questions. In test A, signs and notices with true-or-false statements and a personal letter with questions; in test B, short articles and opinions to match to people, with up to five options.
All 25 questions in 60 minutes, a split of the shared time that Glossa sets because NAEC does not publish one.
Test A: six short facts, as on a form, then a short text and a longer letter. Test B: two argued texts of 10 and 15 points.
All the writing tasks in 50 minutes, rated by AI against NAEC's published criteria.
Three tasks, such as talking about your day (test A) or discussing a topic along three points (test B).
Not included: Glossa has no speech assessment for Georgian.
sections.note: Based on Government Decree No. 418 of 24 September 2025 and NAEC's published test descriptions, sample tasks and scoring schemes for the first session on 6 December 2025, checked in November 2026. NAEC sets the format, the number of tasks and the time before each session, so it can change; at that check no 2026 session had been announced. Look at naec.ge before you register.

sections.heading: What each level needs
sections.intro: A level needs both a total of the 100 points and a minimum in every part, speaking included. A part below its minimum fails that level whatever the total.
items: A1 or B1: 41 points or more, and at least 9 in listening, 11 in reading, 7 in writing and 7 in speaking.
A2 or B2: 61 points or more, and at least 14 in listening, 16 in reading, 12 in writing and 12 in speaking.

sections.heading: Papers to practise on, and a course to learn from

items.title: Two papers for each test
items.text: Four papers in all, full length in listening, reading and writing, with original texts and recordings on everyday life in Georgia: shops, transport, a doctor, a flat, work, travel and the regions.

items.title: Writing rated against the criteria
items.text: Your texts are rated by AI against NAEC's published writing criteria, with what to improve. It is an estimate, not an examiner's mark.

items.title: A full course behind the papers
items.text: 76 modules in eight tiers from the Mkhedruli script to C1, with the ergative, the screeves, preverbs and object marking explained directly, so a weak spot in a paper has a module to go back to.

items.title: Feedback that says why
items.text: Every answer in the course gets feedback with a reason and a link to the grammar rule. Every Georgian word can be tapped for its forms, meaning and audio.

sections.heading: How the practice papers differ from the real exam
items: No level is given. A paper shows the share of points in each part. Test A papers check each part against the A2 minimum, and test B papers against the B1 minimums; the real total includes speaking, which Glossa cannot count, so a paper cannot tell you which level you would reach.
There is no speaking part, although it is 25 of the 100 points.
Reading and writing are timed separately, 60 and 50 minutes. The real test gives them 110 minutes together with no published split.

Some task types are Glossa's. NAEC publishes sample tasks and answer keys, not the full tests, so beyond the samples the mix of tasks is Glossa's, with the real test's numbers of questions and options.
Word counts follow the published samples where there are any; the others are Glossa's.
Recordings can be replayed. In the exam you hear each one twice, so play it twice and then answer.
You choose and type answers on screen, and words can be tapped for their meaning; in the exam you mark a paper answer sheet.

items.question: Is Glossa an official preparation course for the State Language Exam?
items.answer: No. Glossa is not connected with NAEC or the State Language Department. The papers follow NAEC's published test descriptions and scoring schemes, with original content. NAEC's own sample tasks and recordings are on naec.ge; work through them too.

items.question: Do these papers prepare for the Georgian citizenship test?
items.answer: No. People applying for Georgian citizenship take a separate test of the state language at the Public Service Development Agency, whose tasks are not published. The authorities that decide on citizenship set that test and the other conditions.

items.question: Which test should I take, A or B?
items.answer: Test A certifies A1 or A2 and test B certifies B1 or B2. In the course, tiers 1–4 cover A1–A2 and tiers 5–7 B1–B2; the placement test shows where you are.

items.question: What is free?
items.answer: The whole Georgian course from the script to C1, the grammar reference and word practice are free. The exam papers, conversation practice, stories and the other extras are part of Premium.
